summary:
Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework on gender identity and sexual orientation. The sources identify no voivodeship-specific statute, court practice or detention-facility rule departing from it, so the national standards set out below are what a trans visitor here actually faces.

Detention is the clearest documented risk. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement in such a centre wherever a stay would threaten the person's life or health, or wherever the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Border Guard refused to move or release her despite that bar, and she was released only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander; the case page was updated on 28 March 2024.

Custodial healthcare is governed by a binding international ruling. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights by denying hormone replacement therapy to a trans woman held in Siedlce prison, holding that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate, and awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged breaches of Article 3 and Article 14 undecided. The judgment binds Poland as a whole, so it sets the standard for any Polish detention a trans visitor enters while in this voivodeship.

Placement in Polish custody remains individual and unpredictable. Poland operates no specialised section for trans prisoners, and the March 2024 case shows that a statutory bar on unsafe placement did not prevent the placement itself.

Entry is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among the reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.
tangentialFactors:
The surrounding legal environment is unsettled, which bears on how much protection machinery a visitor can expect to reach. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024.

Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation. A March draft amendment to the Penal Code raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Both documented episodes ended in relief obtained outside the ordinary administration: the detained woman was released only after an NGO application to the Border Guard Post commander, and the medication denial was corrected through a Strasbourg judgment. Denial of medication in Polish custody is therefore litigable and winnable, but the two cases together suggest a visitor should not expect an agency to act correctly on first contact.

Canada's advisory placing sexual orientation beside physical appearance and foreigner status as motives for harassment indicates the exposure is not confined to identity documents or presentation alone.
localsOnly:
Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially for residents. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad.

In September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights and called for a recognition framework.

The Article 8 judgment governs healthcare for trans people in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, so a resident in custody here is covered by the same standard a visitor would invoke, with EUR 8,000 available as damages in the precedent case.

Announced hate-speech protection covering gender identity and sexual orientation would apply to residents' daily life, and the Prosecutor General's special response team and law-enforcement guidelines are directed at that domestic conduct.

National law also bars placement of any person in a guarded centre where a stay would threaten life or health or where signs of past violence are present; residents subject to immigration or custodial placement in this voivodeship fall under the same provision.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no enforcement data for Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship itself. Which local court or guarded centre handled a trans foreigner's placement here, how often the statutory placement bar is invoked in this voivodeship, and whether the Border Guard's practice changed after 13 March 2024 are unresolved and not sourced.

Whether the March 2024 detention case arose within Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship is not established by the sources; it is cited as the documented national pattern.

The status of the March and October 2024 Penal Code bills is unresolved at the sources' dates and should be verified before travel rather than assumed either way.

Unsourced: whether guarded centres now supply hormone therapy as a routine matter, or whether any systemic instruction followed the Border Guard commander's intervention in the individual case.

Whether Poland has since enacted a partnership recognition framework in response to the September 2024 ruling is likewise unresolved; no implementing instrument appears in the sources.

No data is available on conviction rates or sentences for anti-trans hate crime, so the practical deterrent value of the pending penalties increase cannot be assessed from these materials.
